newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Strike overshadows record Chrysler profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Strike overshadows record Chrysler profits.

text.p: Hours after reporting record first quarter earnings of $1.029 billion, Chrysler Corp. said Thursday an engine plant strike will force it to halt production of its most profitable light truck models.

The automaker said it will idle four assembly plants starting Friday, including its pickup truck plants in Warren, Mich., and St. Louis, its Jeep Grand Cherokee plant in Detroit and its full-size van plant in Windsor, Ontario.

About 1,800 members of UAW Local 51 struck Chrysler's Mound Road engine plant in Detroit early Thursday in a dispute over jobs and the proposed shifting of work to outside contractors. The plant is the sole U.S. source for the V-6, V-8 and V-10 truck engines that power its Dodge Ram and Dakota pickup trucks, the Grand Cherokee and the Dodge Ram Van.
Higher sales volumes of those same vehicles helped to boost Chrysler's first quarter net by 2.4 percent from the $1.005 billion it earned in the first quarter of 1996.

Chrysler said its first-quarter earnings per share rose to $1.45, slightly exceeding the $1.43 consensus Wall Street estimate compiled by First Call Corp. Chrysler earned $1.30 a share in the year-earlier period, when it had a higher number of shares outstanding.

But Chrysler's future profits could be reduced by about $67 million, or 10 cents a share, per week if production of Grand Cherokees and Ram and Dakota pickups remains halted by the strike, said Burnham Securities analyst David Healy.
"This suggests that they ought to get busy and settle it," he said. "That's production that they probably won't be able to make up, because those plants have been running flat-out."
The automaker's stock was unchanged at $30 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Workers at the Mound Road plant, where the local contract expired at 11:59 p.m. Wednesday, struck to protest plans by Chrysler to shift production of drive shafts to outside suppliers, a move that will cost the plant up to 300 jobs.
The facility also was snubbed on Wednesday when Chrysler announced $1.3 billion in new investments at six other Detroit plants. Plans to phase out its V-8 engines has left its future uncertain.

Analysts said Chrysler's first quarter earnings would have been higher had the company not booked much of the cost of a new minivan incentive program against first quarter earnings. The move to place a $595 incentive on four-door vans already on dealer lots reduced first quarter pre-tax income by more than $100 million.
The move also pushed Chrysler's incentive levels up to $785 per vehicle at the end of the quarter. The average for the quarter was $705, up from $640 a year ago.
"Competition for the consumer's automotive dollar got increasingly intense in the first quarter," Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said in a statement.

He added that Chrysler remains optimistic about the spring selling season, despite pressure from Japanese automakers that is being fueled by the weakness of the yen against the dollar and strong new products.

Chrysler posted total first quarter revenues of $16.12 billion, up from $14.96 billion. Worldwide factory unit shipments to dealers rose by 3.7 percent to 781,239 vehicles from 753,176 a year earlier.

Chrysler Chief Financial Officer Gary Valade said the automaker has underscored its confidence in the strength of the economy by planning its strongest second quarter production in 20 years, a total of 818,200 vehicles. He said he did not believe small increases in interest rates will reduce vehicle demand.
"We see the economy in the best fundamental shape that it's been in in the last 25 years or so," Valade said. "That's good for the auto business."
